name: Kitja (Gija), glottocode kitj1240, Jarrakan
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding fixed-strict initial (initial stress). (1) Quote check: the record held no file; I downloaded the deciding source (Babinski 2022 diss.) and the quotation is verbatim at p.27; the Babinski 2026 JIPA corroboration is verbatim in a copies we hold. (2) The classification rests on a 2022 dissertation relaying the sole primary phonology sketch (Taylor & Taylor 1971:108) plus a 2026 JIPA instrumental study that finds f0, intensity, vowel-duration and onset-lengthening correlates on the initial syllable in Gija; against Glottolog's list (one 1971 phonology sketch, one 1996 learner's grammar, a 2022 dictionary, a phrasebook) and the LDD 2020 snapshot's own survey, nothing better on Gija stress exists, and nothing seen suggests non-initial stress (Jarrakan/Kimberley languages are uniformly described as initial-stress). sources.citation: Babinski 2022:27 (Archival Phonetics & Prosodic Typology in Sixteen Australian Languages, Yale PhD dissertation; full PDF text read via EliScholar through r.jina.ai after direct 403), which quotes the primary description Taylor & Taylor 1971:108 with page number; plus Babinski 2026 (Stress in Austr…
sources.quote: Babinski 2022:27: "A short description of Gija stress was presented in Taylor & Taylor (1971: 108), who note that stress in 'normal intonation' falls on the initial syllable of the word." Corroborated by Babinski 2026 (JIPA), selection criterion: "Only languages with a documented description of fixed and word initial lexical stress are considered here, for consistency in comparing phonetic cues" (Gija included; her acoustic study confirms stress correlates on the initial syllable).

sources.citation: Babinski, Sarah. 2022. Archival Phonetics & Prosodic Typology in Sixteen Australian Languages. PhD dissertation, Yale University. EliScholar gsas_dissertations/556 (248 pp).
sources.quote: p.27: 'A short description of Gija stress was presented in Taylor & Taylor (1971: 108), who note that stress in "normal intonation" falls on the initial syllable of the word.' Sec. 5.4: f0 is a significant correlate of (initial) stress in Gija (~1 semitone), duration significant for 2 of 5 speakers.

sources.quote: No stress statement. Confirms the descriptive landscape: 'in the 1970s, brief descriptions were provided of its phonology (Taylor & Taylor 1971)'; Kofod 1996 is characterised as 'a learner's sketch grammar'; the only academic publications on Gija are in semantics and historical linguistics.
